chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked
about a man who killed a believer while knowing he was a believer, except that anger drove him to kill him — is there repentance for him if he intends it, or is there no repentance for him?

He said: Retaliation is applied to him. And if it is not publicly known, he should go to his (victim's) guardians and inform them that he killed him. If they forgive him, he shall give them the blood money, emancipate a slave, fast for two consecutive months, and give charity to sixty poor persons.

key_terms.أَوْلِيَاء: Awliya' — guardians or next-of-kin who hold the right to either demand qisas, accept diyah, or grant pardon
key_terms.الدِّيَةَ: Diyah (blood money) — a prescribed financial compensation paid to the victim's family in lieu of retaliation
key_terms.رَقَبَةً: Raqabah — literally 'a neck'; Islamic legal term for freeing a slave as an act of expiation (kaffarah)
key_terms.يُقَادُ: Qisas — the principle of retaliation in Islamic law, where the killer faces the same fate as the victim

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation (kaffarah) for killing a believer in anger in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) addresses the legal ruling for a believer who kills another believer in a fit of anger with full knowledge of the victim's faith. The Imam specifies a graduated path of expiation: first, qisas (retaliation) is the primary right; if the matter is not publicly known, the killer must voluntarily confess to the victim's family; if they pardon him, he must still fulfill three acts of kaffarah — paying the diyah (blood money), freeing a slave, fasting sixty consecutive days, and feeding sixty poor persons. This is situated in the broader Quranic discourse on the gravity of killing a believer (Quran 4:93) while simultaneously providing a path for repentance through restorative justice to the victim's family and acts of worship.
